title: Bill Boyd's band: playing the blues, instrumentation and records
summary: Crowds waited for the solo choruses on St. Louis Blues, and tunes were played twice in a row. The band had two guitars, bass, two violins, banjo and piano, and Parker recorded with Boyd later, after joining the Doughboys.

story.theme_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section: instruments and players
story.community_name: Who played what: early band size and instrumentation

blocks.x: Well, I think the Tate could take us. How's it happen that you joined a band like Bill Boyd? I mean, you were a musician.

Well, that was the band that was playing there, and they liked all the, oh, that's what they mainly liked, and whenever we'd play old St. Louis blues and some little old dive there, and I'd take three or four courses, people would come around there, they'd stand around, you see, and they would stop the kind of whole show and take two or three more courses and play the thing. In those days, we would play one tune and stop for a few seconds and then play the same tune again because their repertoire was limited, and we'd play one tune twice, once right after the other. And they'd wait for the courses to come up again and just stand around and watch, and the guitarist was terrific, too. Oh, he was a knockout old Jim Boyd. Played very well, very, very well. And they'd wait for these, for the soloists they'd like, especially the crowd around there, and they'd have a ball. How large a band was this? Oh, there were about two guitars, one of them was a solo and no one of the accompaniments, bass, two violins, banjo, piano. What kind of banjo was that? Now, I don't remember the banjos with Bill Boyd. I don't remember him at all. The banjos that I remember primarily is Marvin Montgomery, the Larkless Dole Boys, who was one of the greatest, oh, banjo pickers of all time, anywhere.
Did you make records with Bill Boyd?
That was before you had, before you had joined Blackie Simmons.

No, wait a minute. When I was with Bill Boyd, there were just a few odd dancers, and I'd go up there and play with him on the radio program for about a week. When I first went there to Dallas, just before joining over, moving over, and taking the pianist's place, for whom Bill Boyd had already contracted, before I appeared on the scene. During his two weeks' notice, I appeared up there and played with Bill Boyd. Then you switched with him.
And then you came back with Bill Boyd.
Much later on for record dates, yes.
Was that before joining the Larkless Dole Boys?
No, after joining the Dole Boys. After that. Yes.
